Area.evidence_source: More than half had told stories of childhood/adolescence characterized by considerable difficulty: illness, loss of close relatives and poverty. 'They had to manage on their own,' the informants said about several of them. Six of the 23 subjects lost one of their parents at an early age (four as infants), three also lost siblings (one through suicide) in their youth. Several had felt rejected by step-parents, and talked of a lack of care after one of the parents died. Many grew up under poor conditions in large families: 'Those who were going to school had to have the clothes without holes.' Illness marked two of them early in life: one had to spend two years in infancy at a tuberculosis sanatorium far away from home. Many of the elderly had acquired education for themselves despite limited financial resources. Three enlisted for active service at a young age. They experienced, and seemed to cope with, severe loss also later in life. Seven of them had lost their spouse relatively early, and three had experienced losing children, one losing two sons in accidents. One who suffered from a serious chronic illness throughout his life looked after four children, two of whom were handicapped, when he found himself alone with them. In the interviews many of the elderly emerged as 'survivors'. Poverty and emotional deprivation on the part of caregivers in childhood did not prevent them from functioning well as adults. They also coped with stress later in adulthood.
